# njoagleod

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/tor-gu/njoagleod/workflows/R-CMD-check/badge.svg)](https://github.com/tor-gu/njoagleod/actions)
<!-- badges: end -->

This is a cleaned-up version of the NJ OAG Law Enforcement Officer Diversity
  database available from https://www.njoag.gov/policerecruiting/

## Dataset Overview
This package is built from the 2025 NJ OAG release, which covers officers for
2021--2025 and agencies and applicants for 2022--2025. It contains three tables.

* ```agency_practice``` Each agency's hiring and promotion practices, by year.
* ```officer``` Counts of officers by year, agency, race, age range, gender and promotion.
* ```applicant``` Counts of applicants by year, agency, race, age range, gender, applicant
  type and outcome.

The tables identify agencies by ```agency_id```, a stable identifier from the
[```njlea```](https://github.com/tor-gu/njlea) registry of NJ law enforcement agencies.
This package re-exports njlea's functions for looking agencies up:

* ```get_agencies(year)``` The agencies in a year, with their names as of that year,
  county, level and function.
* ```get_agency_municipalities(year)``` The municipalities each agency serves, identified as
  in the [```njmunicipalities```](https://github.com/tor-gu/njmunicipalities) package.
* ```find_agency(pattern)``` Search agency names and every source spelling.

njlea's tables (```njlea::agency```, ```njlea::agency_alias``` and the others) have the
full registry.

## Examples
```{r, message = FALSE}
library(njoagleod)
library(dplyr)
```

The agencies in 2025:
```{r}
get_agencies(2025)
```

The ```officer``` and ```applicant``` tables are count tables: each row is a combination of
characteristics, and ```officer_count``` (or ```applicant_count```) is the number of people
who share it.
```{r}
officer
```
So count people with the count as a weight. Counting rows counts combinations, not officers.
```{r}
officer |>
  filter(year == 2025) |>
  count(officer_race, wt = officer_count, name = "officers")
```

An agency's name can change from year to year, so to attach names to a table that covers
several years, get each year's agencies and join on ```agency_id``` and ```year```:
```{r}
agency_names <- function(years) {
  bind_rows(lapply(years, function(y) mutate(get_agencies(y), year = y)))
}

officer |>
  count(year, agency_id, wt = officer_count, name = "officers") |>
  left_join(agency_names(2021:2025), by = c("agency_id", "year")) |>
  select(year, county, agency_name, officers) |>
  arrange(desc(officers))
```

### Municipalities
```get_agency_municipalities()``` lists the municipalities each agency serves, with their
names and GEOIDs as of the year asked for:
```{r}
get_agency_municipalities(2025) |>
  left_join(get_agencies(2025) |> select(agency_id, agency_name), by = "agency_id") |>
  select(agency_name, GEOID, county, municipality, link_type)
```
Agencies that serve more than one municipality have one row for each:
```{r}
get_agencies(2025) |>
  filter(multi_municipal) |>
  inner_join(get_agency_municipalities(2025), by = "agency_id",
             suffix = c("_agency", "")) |>
  select(agency_name, municipality, link_type)
```

### Use with ```njoaguof```
The [```njoaguof```](https://github.com/tor-gu/njoaguof) use-of-force package uses the same
```agency_id```, so use-of-force incidents can be set against what this package knows about
each agency: its officers and its hiring practices. Here we count 2024 incidents per agency.
```{r}
incidents_2024 <- njoaguof::incident |>
  filter(format(incident_date_1, "%Y") == "2024") |>
  count(agency_id, name = "incidents")
```
From the ```officer``` table, the size of each agency's force and its share of female
officers and of officers aged 35 or under; from ```agency_practice```, whether hiring is
governed by Civil Service.
```{r}
officers_2024 <- officer |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  group_by(agency_id) |>
  summarize(
    officers = sum(officer_count),
    pct_female = 100 * sum(officer_count[officer_gender %in% "Female"]) / officers,
    pct_35_or_under =
      100 * sum(officer_count[officer_age_range %in% c("25 or less", "26-35")]) / officers
  )

agency_2024 <- officers_2024 |>
  left_join(incidents_2024, by = "agency_id") |>
  mutate(incidents = coalesce(incidents, 0L),
         incidents_per_100_officers = 100 * incidents / officers) |>
  left_join(agency_practice |> filter(year == 2024) |>
              select(agency_id, hiring_civil_service),
            by = "agency_id") |>
  left_join(get_agencies(2024) |> select(agency_id, agency_name, agency_level),
            by = "agency_id")
```
The ten agencies with at least 50 officers and the most incidents per officer:
```{r}
agency_2024 |>
  filter(officers >= 50) |>
  arrange(desc(incidents_per_100_officers)) |>
  select(agency_name, officers, pct_female, pct_35_or_under, hiring_civil_service,
         incidents_per_100_officers) |>
  head(10) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 0)
```
And, for municipal agencies, incidents per 100 officers by Civil Service hiring and by the
share of officers aged 35 or under:
```{r}
agency_2024 |>
  filter(agency_level == "Municipal") |>
  mutate(pct_35_or_under = cut(pct_35_or_under, c(0, 30, 45, 60, 100),
                               include.lowest = TRUE)) |>
  group_by(hiring_civil_service, pct_35_or_under) |>
  summarize(agencies = n(),
            incidents_per_100_officers = 100 * sum(incidents) / sum(officers),
            .groups = "drop")
```
These are descriptive only: incident rates depend heavily on what each agency polices, and
some agencies' officer counts are incomplete (see the note below).

## Notes
These are the ways in which this package differs from the source data.

### Agencies
The source identifies agencies by county and name only. The ```agency_id```, the agency
names, levels and functions, and the municipalities served all come from
[```njlea```](https://github.com/tor-gu/njlea), not from the source. njlea uses its own
canonical names (such as "Absecon Police Department" for the source's "Absecon City PD"),
records every source spelling in ```njlea::agency_alias``` (source
```"njoag-leod-2025"```), and documents its corrections to the source, such as the
municipalities served under shared-services agreements. ```find_agency()``` searches the
names and the source spellings. The source's "Chester PD", for instance, is Chester
Township's department:
```{r}
find_agency("^Chester PD$")
```

### Incomplete agency reports
The data is as reported by each agency, and some agency-years look incomplete. For example,
Lakewood PD reports 153 officers in 2021 but 20 in 2022 and 58 in 2025, and Saddle Brook PD
reports about 30 officers every year until 2025, when it reports 5. This package does not
correct these. Here are the agency-years with fewer than half the agency's median number of
officers (among agencies with a median of at least 10). This is only a rough screen: it misses
agencies that report too few officers in most years, such as Fair Lawn PD, which reports 7 to
17 officers in 2021--2024 and 56 in 2025.
```{r}
officer |>
  count(agency_id, year, wt = officer_count, name = "officers") |>
  group_by(agency_id) |>
  mutate(median_officers = median(officers)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(median_officers >= 10, officers < median_officers / 2) |>
  left_join(agency_names(2021:2025), by = c("agency_id", "year")) |>
  select(year, county, agency_name, officers, median_officers) |>
  arrange(year, county, agency_name) |>
  print(n = Inf)
```

### Recoded values
"Not Provided" and "Blank" are recoded as `NA`, and yes/no answers as logicals. One value in
the source has a trailing space (`"Other "` as the reason for no appointment), which has been
removed.

## Installation

You can install the latest version of njoagleod from [GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

``` r
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("tor-gu/njoagleod")
```
